title: Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: Connect the Dots: Training LLMs for Long-Lifecycle Agents with Cross-Domain Generalization Via Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract This work presents a general framework for training large language models (LLMs) to “ Co nnect the D ots” ( CoD ), a meta-capability required by long-lifecycle agents:
as an LLM-based AI agent gets deployed in an environment, it solves a long sequence of tasks while continuously exploring the environment, learning from its own experiences, and iteratively self-updating its context about the environment, thereby achieving progressively better performance on future tasks conditioned on the updated context.
Major components of the CoD framework include:
(1) algorithm design and infrastructure for end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) with long rollout sequences interleaving solve-task and update-context episodes;
(2) tasks and environments for incentivizing and eliciting the targeted meta-capability in LLMs during training, as well as for faithfully measuring progress during evaluation.
We present proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework,
including a GRPO-style RL algorithm with fine-grained credit assignment,
as well as tasks and environments tailored to the targeted meta-capability (rather than domain-specific LLM capabilities or standard task-by-task RL).
Empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL training in the CoD setting,
and demonstrate the potential for out-of-distribution generalization —
within the training domains, across different domains, and from CoD to Ralph-loop settings
— of the elicited meta-capability.
Our investigation of CoD connects several lines of prior works,
and opens up new opportunities for advancing LLMs and AI agents.
To facilitate further research and applications,
we release our implementations at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/research/cod/examples/research_cod .

Work done during an internship at Alibaba Group. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have progressed rapidly in the past few years, evolving from chatbots to reasoning models, and now serving as the backbones for numerous AI agents in real-world applications. We envision that in the near future, further progress in LLMs will bring them to long-lifecycle agentic deployment in diverse environments and continual learning at test time . To achieve this vision, an AI agent should be able to “ Co nnect the D ots” ( CoD ). More formally, we define the CoD meta-capability as follows: during long-lifecycle deployment in an environment , an AI agent continuously solves a sequence of different-but-related tasks , while proactively and deliberately exploring the environment and self-updating its context about it, thereby facilitating more effective task solving within the same environment in the future. In contrast to domain-specific capabilities (such as math problem solving and competitive coding), CoD is a meta-capability that can potentially generalize across diverse environments from different domains, enabling the AI agent to self-improve efficiently during deployment and thereby enhancing its task-solving performance ( Silver and Sutton, 2025 ; Rafiee and Sutton, 2026 ) . Frontier LLMs today still fall short in this regard: with limited CoD meta-capability, an LLM-based agent may easily get lost in environments with underspecification ( Laban et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2025 ) , and often requires human-crafted agent scaffolds with sophisticated design in order to operate stably over a long lifecycle. We believe that LLMs need to be explicitly trained for the CoD meta-capability, ideally through end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) in environments with clean reward signals. Indeed, while early LLMs exhibited certain chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Kojima et al., 2022 ) and agentic intelligence ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , reinforcement learning — with properly designed algorithms and environments — has proved effective in driving fundamental improvements in these aspects ( OpenAI, 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Kimi-Team, 2025 ; Qwen-Team, 2026 ; Kimi-Team, 2026 ; GLM-5-Team, 2026 ) ; we anticipate that the same should hold for eliciting the CoD meta-capability in LLMs. On the other hand, standard task-by-task RL essentially trains an LLM to solve each task individually from scratch , which appears misaligned with the CoD meta-capability targeted for long-lifecycle deployment. This motivates us to design and implement a dedicated RL process for CoD ; in this work, we present our initial progress. Contributions and organization. We begin by introducing a general CoD framework, visualized in Figure 1 and elaborated in Section 2 . CoD-Deploy represents an abstraction of long-lifecycle deployment of an AI agent in an environment, which interleaves episodes for solving new tasks and for self-updating the agent’s context about the environment. CoD-Train denotes the corresponding RL post-training process, whose rollout pattern exactly matches that of CoD-Deploy . One major challenge lies in RL algorithm design, and in particular, credit assignment across solve-task and update-context episodes in a long state-action sequence. We adopt the classical dynamic-programming principle ( Bellman, 1957 ; Sutton et al., 1998 ) : the objective of each episode is to maximize not only the immediate reward, but also future rewards. Another major challenge is the choice of appropriate tasks and environments ( Huang et al., 2025 ) . For training, we need environments that properly incentivize self-updating an agent’s context about the environment — e.g., revealed clues that were initially hidden, or task-solving skills with validated efficacy — and solving new tasks conditioned on that context rather than from scratch. For evaluation, we need environments that faithfully measure progress in improving the CoD meta-capability of LLMs. The CoD framework therefore calls for dedicated task and environment design, as standard RL datasets and LLM benchmarks are not necessarily suitable for these purposes. In an effort to tackle these challenges, we present in Section 3 our concrete implementations of the CoD framework, which include RL algorithms and infrastructure, along with environments and tasks tailored to CoD . Our empirical results validate the efficacy of end-to-end RL for eliciting the CoD meta-capability. For example, when applying CoD-Train to Qwen3-8B-Instruct on FrozenLake-Obscure environments containing clues that are necessary for successful task solving but initially hidden, the agent’s success rate in solving a task from scratch rises only from 18% to 45% (approximately) due to information-theoretic limits, yet its success rate in solving the fourth task within a sequence — conditioned on its self-updated context — increases substantially from 28% to 76%. Moreover, the elicited CoD meta-capability demonstrates potential for in-domain and cross-domain generalization, as well as generalization to Ralph-loop settings ( Huntley, 2026 ) , as validated by out-of-distribution evaluation. During our development of CoD , we connect several lines of prior work, including research and practice of “lifelong agents” ( Workshop, 2026a ) , meta reinforcement learning ( Duan et al., 2016 ) , inference scaling ( Huntley, 2026 ) , among others. A brief review of these lines, along with their connections to and differences from CoD , can be found in Section 4 . Finally, while this work provides proof-of-concept implementations of the CoD framework and presents promising empirical results, many research questions remain open and call for further work, e.g., refining the design of RL algorithms and environments dedicated to CoD , continuing to scale up CoD along various dimensions, and integrating CoD into existing LLM post-training pipelines; detailed discussions can be found in Section 5 . Figure 1 : A visualization of CoD-Deploy and CoD-Train (compared with standard task-by-task RL), where A A and B B denote different environments for training, and M M denotes a new environment for deployment or evaluation. Each block represents one rollout episode for solving a task x i x_{i} (which could be in itself a long-horizon multi-turn task) or updating the agent’s context z i z_{i} about the current environment. 2 The CoD framework In this section, we introduce the CoD framework — visualized in Figure 1 — that aims for eliciting the aforementioned CoD meta-capability in LLMs via RL post-training. • CoD-Deploy is an abstraction of long-lifecycle agentic deployment in an environment M M , which interleaves episodes for solving a task x i M x_{i}^{M} and for updating the agent’s context from z i M z_{i}^{M} to z i + 1 M z_{i+1}^{M} . This process can be understood as (gradient-free) online learning via trial-and-errors. • CoD-Train represents the rollout mechanism in RL post-training dedicated to CoD , and the corresponding RL algorithm for training model weights. Note that the rollout pattern in CoD-Train is simply the same as in CoD-Deploy , covering diverse environments A , B , … A,B,\dots for generalization. From the perspective of hierarchical reinforcement learning , CoD-Train goes up by one level in the hierarchy, compared to standard task-by-task RL. Indeed, the definition of one rollout trajectory in LLM-RL has evolved from a sequence of tokens for a single-turn task (e.g., RLHF ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ) and reasoning-oriented RLVR ( OpenAI, 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) ), to a sequence of turns for a long-horizon agentic task ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) ; CoD-Train takes it one step further, to a sequence of tasks for long-lifecycle agentic deployment in an environment. End-to-end reinforcement learning. Given the problem formulation in CoD-Train , we aim for effective end-to-end RL training. One crucial aspect here is credit assignment for a long state-action sequence consisting of multiple solve-task and update-context episodes, each of which might already contain multiple turns of agent-environment interaction and thus a large number of tokens. Fortunately, we have one critical observation: suppose that there is (at least) an outcome reward for solving each task, then the total number of reward values in the end-to-end state-action sequence will grow proportionally with the number of tasks, i.e., the density of reward signals is independent of the total number of tasks. We follow the fundamental dynamic-programming principle ( Bellman, 1957 ; Sutton et al., 1998 ) for credit assignment in CoD-Train : each episode should aim for maximizing not only the immediate reward, but also future rewards. In an update-context episode, the agent performs deliberate condensation of its previous experiences and incorporate it into the updated context, which should contribute to better performance in solving future tasks within the same environment.
